Would suggest to break this down into one a category of checks per patch.

Which will make it easier to get a larger number of upvotes from different subproject maintainers.

Otherwise it will be hard for people to find the time to look into the implications of each of those checks.

Then we are just dumping a huge list here without any alignment from the people who are supposed to be reviewing the changes to enable those checks.

I would really rather do what I put in the commit message, and remove any patches that people believe shouldn't be enabled in this first batch, then open the rest on a case by case basis.  FWIW, a lot of the checks go by two different names (cert-* specifically), so I don't want to bifurcate conversations to two different reviews if one of those comes up.

To some extent, these are the checks that subproject groups have already (even if implicitly) agreed on in some of the larger repos (bmcweb, dbus-sensors).  If we break it up, we lose that this is essentially the same list that's already use today and we know to be functional.  So if it's ok, I'd really prefer not breaking it up.  If other folks don't want to use the existing check list as a starting point for this review, we can go a different route.
@alexander.hansen@9elements.com Are you ok with the above?  I will remove any checks that you think shouldn't be included.
provided my feedback about these checks 👍

I appreciate the feedback, but I'm struggling a bit because almost every answer is "this check has been turned on for years and has been proven to work in our codebase".  Almost every case where YES, it COULD be valid, but the point is that it's far more likely to be LESS valid.

I would really prefer to use this as a starting point.  If you really want me to move some of the below out, can you prioritize the ones that we can actually show are harmful?  Or do you really need ALL removed?

> I'm struggling a bit because almost every answer is "this check has been turned on for years and has been proven to work in our codebase". 

+1. 

This seems like a solid starting point to me.

> I would really prefer to use this as a starting point. If you really want me to move some of the below out, can you prioritize the ones that we can actually show are harmful? Or do you really need ALL removed?

Based on your experience you will know which checks work well. I closed most of my comments since i don't have that strong of an opinion here.

I thought we wanted to come up with a subset of these where the work would be minimal to enable them. If you want to do the work to enable all these checks on most of the repos, more power to you.

Otherwise someone else will have to enable them, right? It's not `tidy-desired.md`.

These are essentially the checks that have broad adoption already, and have been shown to work on our code across multiple repos, so at least the way I had defined tidy-desired, that's not where these would go.

Let's see how far these checks go and who will do work to enable them.

I would suggest we look for a few +1 from people who maintain projects that do not already have these checks enabled.

If there is any broad adoption of these checks i would also expect to see a +1 from a number of people who already enabled them for their repos.

That being said, nothing blocking this change from my side, we went over all the checks i had some minor concerns about.
Do we really want to encourage this?  It seems like it tends to lead to lots of NOLINT adds.
I think it's better than not enabling the check at all, but it is a judgement call on how much mess it makes.  We could remove the documentation of NOLINT from here if you'd prefer.
I removed it for now.  Lets resolve in the next patches.

I'd like to point maintainers to using `config-clang-tidy` for rolling this out to their repos.  By default it disables all the checks but leaves them commented in and in place.  They can then use the tool to enable them one-by-one.

When we add new checks to the list it becomes programmatic to run the tool to apply the new check to all existing .clang-tidy files.
Sure, I can add a reference to that tool here.
Added a reference.

I might put up a patch on top of this of additional opinions on these.  Some of them, especially in the "stylistic-*" I don't like and don't think they match our coding standards.  We can discuss how to merge them together after that.

That sounds great.  Things like enforcing the upper or lower casing of uint literals (1u vs 1U) is one I could for sure do without, but I honestly haven't taken the time to look up what check that is and disable it.  I'm sure there's more we probably agree on.

2. Some folks questioned why we had certain cert checks disabled, and it was easier to just have the duplicate than have to explain why we were "avoiding cert guidelines"

With that said, i think both those reasons are mediocre, so I will go through and deduplicate.  ACK

Instead of listing 300+ individual checks explicitly, consider switching to a hybrid .clang-tidy configuration using wildcard-based groups with targeted exclusions.
This keeps the config cleaner, easier to maintain, and future-proof—especially as clang-tidy evolves and new checks are added under existing groups.

Eg:
Checks: >
  clang-analyzer-*,
  bugprone-*,
  performance-*,
  modernize-*,
  readability-*,
  -modernize-use-trailing-return-type,
  -readability-magic-numbers,
I intentionally didn't do that because each version of tidy adds new checks, and I don't want the codebase to immediately start failing on new versions.
The same issue can occur even with explicitly listed checks—if a newer clang-tidy version deprecates or modifies existing checks, the config may still break or behave unexpectedly.

No, it doesn't.  The couple checks that were deprecated are still accepted they now just do nothing.  If there are modifications to existing checks, yes, we sometimes have that problem, but that's different than new checks.  Also new checks tend to be less stable.  I don't agree with the argument that "it's still possible so we should allow the problem to be worse".  Adding new checks takes time.  I as a maintainer don't want to sign up to go add new check support and fix everything immediately on a clang release.

Totally get your concern about wildcard groups pulling in unstable new checks after a clang-tidy version bump.
But just to note—explicitly listing 300+ checks doesn’t fully avoid that risk either. Existing checks can change behavior or get deprecated silently, which can still break builds or reduce coverage.
The hybrid approach keeps things clean and scalable, and we can always disable noisy new checks explicitly (-check-name) if they cause issues.

> explicitly listing 300+ checks doesn’t fully avoid that risk either.

Agreed, but it SIGNIFICANTLY reduces the problem to the point where it's not a burden.  Clang isn't in in the business of messing with checks that work and function correctly, and while this concern is real, I haven't personally seen this outside of a few minor cases.

> we can always disable noisy new checks

This is something the maintainer now has to proactively evaluate.  Just to show my concern, the workflow with this file as in the review is:

Fix compiler warnings -> upgrade clang -> enable new check (per repo).

If we wildcard this, now clang updates becomes:

Fix new compiler warnings -> fix check in all N repositories -> upgrade clang.
@ojayanth@gmail.com does that answer your question on why not wildcards?

I agree both approaches have some maintenance cost. Even with explicit listing, we can't fully avoid issues from behavioral changes or silent deprecations in existing checks. I'm happy to go with whatever works best for the team.
👍. Thank you for your response.

For example if we have a local var in `main` function, passing a reference to that var is fine.
Can you give an example in our code?
See below.  This is cpp core guidelines.  Unless we think the check itself doesn't match the intent or guideline, we shouldn't be disabling things that are already documented.

I think that's the point of the check, the code "works", but it's highly likely that reference ends up as a use after free at some point in the future.  I suspect that's the point of the check, to ask you to write that as 

initDevice(std::string service,std::string path, SoftwareConfig config)

To avoid the use after free footgun.

I'm closing the comment since you are technically correct about the issue and the code example has this footgun.

The suggested alternative is also bad since we would be copying everything, but at least it would not crash.

Always initializing a variable can lead to code bloat.

It can lead to a situation where an initial value is set but always overwritten in every code path, which is confusing.

The relevant part is for clang-tidy to figure out if an uninitialized var is used somewhere and there is other checks which can take care of that.

```
    clang-analyzer-core.uninitialized.ArraySubscript,
    clang-analyzer-core.uninitialized.Assign,
    clang-analyzer-core.uninitialized.Branch,
    clang-analyzer-core.uninitialized.NewArraySize,
```

> Always initializing a variable can lead to code bloat.

Please articulate this concern using numbers.  We have not seen this, and it's a very important security issue that we need to catch.

I'd also point out that this is a cpp core guidelines check, which is directly the standard we follow.  if we think this check is inappropriate, we should either:
1. Take this up with cpp core guidelines that we think this is wrong
2. Take this up with OPenBMC that we should ignore cpp core guidelines for this case.
I don't have a strong opinion here. And not enough examples of code where this would be an issue. Closing.
